newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cr Lyonnais sale may not come for couple of years.
newsitem.headline: Cr Lyonnais sale may not come for couple of years.

text.p: Ailing bank Credit Lyonnais, which the French government has vowed to privatise as soon as possible, may take a while to find suitors, industry sources and banking analysts said on Thursday.

"All scenarios are possible but I think it will be a minimum of two years before it is privatised," one source close to the dossier said, adding that it would take that long for Credit Lyonnais's finances to be put on a sound footing.

The European Commission on Wednesday cleared 3.9 billion francs ($759 million) in emergency aid for the bank whose troubles stem from an over-ambitious expansion spree in the 1980s that brought it to the brink of bankruptcy.
At the same time the French government announced it was open to offers for the bank but said it would require another big bailout -- its third in as many years -- in order to be privatised.
The government, which had originally planned to sell the bank by around 2000, said it was ready to consider any proposals from investors for a minority or a majority stake.
Banking analysts were doubtful about who would be interested in the bank, at least in the short-term, because of its low profitability in France's weak banking environment.

"If you're a rich foreign bank or insurer it is a way to be in the French market but you would have to bet on the future profitability of the French market and that's not a sure thing," said one analyst.
"Maybe they should just give every French taxpayer a share," said another, referring to the bank's need for huge amounts of public money to keep it alive.
One analyst estimated that the total bill to taxpayers would be at least 125 billion francs when the final tally is made.

Under the emergency aid package announced on Wednesday, the government will assume costs imposed on the bank as part of last year's bailout. As a result, Credit Lyonnais is expected to be able to post a first profit of several hundred million francs.

Without the emergency aid, the bank, which eked out a profit of 13 billion francs last year after posting losses of 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994, was expected to post a loss of around two billion francs.
The French government said Credit Lyonnais would need further state money but would not say how much it would need to recapitalise the bank until after it releases its results on October 3.
Press reports have suggested that the government may need to inject at least another 10 billion francs into the bank.
One of the names most frequently mentioned as a possible suitor was German insurer Allianz AG whose products are already being sold over Credit Lyonnais's bank counters.
But analysts said it was unlikely Credit Lyonnais' domestic rivals would be interested as the state-controlled bank's extensive retail network would be too large for them to absorb.
The accelerated timetable for the bank's privatisation was seen as a quid pro quo for winning the European Commission's approval for the fresh state aid.
But the Commission is likely to demand that Credit Lyonnais step up its assets sales, especially in Europe, and increase cuts in staff and costs.
The bank's rivals, which had bitterly complained that last year's bailout was too generous, remained silent on Thursday over plans for fresh emergency aid.

Societe Generale chairman Marc Viennot, who was one of the most vociferous critics, has decided he is no longer going to comment on Credit Lyonnais, a spokeswoman there said. ($ = 5.140 French Francs)
